name: Titoism
summary: Titoism is the doctrine and practice of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito after the 1948 break with Stalin. It replaced Soviet-style state ownership and central planning with social ownership, workers' self-management and market socialism, kept a one-party state that called itself socialist democracy, organized Yugoslavia as a federation of equal nations under 'brotherhood and unity', and pursued nonalignment between the Cold War blocs.
scope: The Yugoslav line from the 1948 split to Tito's death in 1980, as its defining sources present it: the 1958 Programme of the League of Communists (named by Benson's encyclopedia entry as the historic statement of 'self-governing socialism'), the 1974 constitution, the speeches of Tito and the theory of Edvard Kardelj, and the regime's record (McVicker 1957; the Library of Congress country study). It excludes the Stalinist 1945-48 phase except as background, the post-1980 republics' divergences, and foreign movements that borrowed the label.

notes: Later pass (rules 5) by claude-opus-5-5. The first pass rested almost wholly on Wikipedia; this pass rebuilt it from the 1958 Programme of the League of Yugoslav Communists, the 1974 constitution, Tito's speeches (1950, 1954, 1957, the 1960 UN address) and Kardelj's Socialism and War, with the regime's record from the Library of Congress country study (1990) and McVicker's 1957 study of the 1950s reforms, and Benson's encyclopedia entry for scope. Record over words: where the regime acted (one-party rule, delegate elections, courts, religion policy, media control, conscription, abortion law, prices, trade, nonalignment) the answer rests on the record or the enacted constitution alone; the Programme answers only where there is no record. Over time: the answers follow the mature line of 1950-1980 (self-management, the 1963 and 1974 constitutions), not the Stalinist 1945-48 phase; where the record moved both ways (market socialism after 1965 and Tito's 1974 recentralization, collectivization abandoned while socialist farms were promoted, the constitutional right of secession against the 1971 Croatian purge) the answer is mixed or low. Every first-pass answer was rechecked; 57 that the new sources do not settle are nulled. Not used: Tito's 1956 speech on Hungary (MIA scan without a text layer), and the lending-only archive.org copies of Yugoslavia's Way (the 1958 Programme in another translation) and Neal's Titoism in Action. Themes searched: economy (ownership, planning, markets, prices, unions, strikes, agriculture, taxes, banking, foreign capital), government (party, elections, delegate system, courts, presidency, federation, rotation, recall), liberty (rights chapter, censorship, dissent, surveillance, death penalty), society (religion, family, women, abortion, education, nationalities and languages), world (nonalignment, blocs, UN, colonialism, aid, disarmament, defence doctrine, conscription), ecology and technology (Programme and constitution only).
